segments.say: The story of Kitty Genovese has been retold in textbooks for sixty years. Thirty-eight people watched a murder from their windows and did nothing. It's a powerful tale. The trouble is that much of it appears to be wrong, and the way it was corrected is a lesson in itself.

show.title: The myth of the silent crowd

segments.say: Two weeks after the killing, The New York Times published a front page article that stated that thirty-eight respectable, law-abiding citizens had watched a killer stalk and stab a woman in three separate attacks, and that not one person telephoned the police. The article was widely read, and it shaped how a generation thought about city life.

Rachael Manning, Mark Levine and Alan Collins went back to the court records and later accounts. They found that the number thirty-eight could not be supported. Few people had a clear view of the attacks, some heard only fragments they took for a quarrel, and at least one witness did call the police. The picture of a crowd of callous watchers was far too simple.

show.what: The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping: the parable of the 38 witnesses

segments.say: The last of these details is the one that stays with people. A neighbour, Sophie Farrar, reached Kitty Genovese in the final moments and held her. The tale of total indifference left out this act, and many others like it. The story endured partly because it was simple and shocking, and not because it was accurate.

show.title: What the later research found
items: The count of thirty-eight was not supported by the records
Most neighbours did not see the whole attack
At least one person called the police
A neighbour, Sophie Farrar, went to comfort the victim

segments.say: Why did the false version spread so widely, and why did it last? Psychologists point out that it fitted what many people already believed about big cities, and it offered a dramatic lesson. A vivid story is often remembered long after the corrections appear, and the corrections reach far fewer readers.

The case is a reminder that our picture of human nature is shaped by stories that may not be true. It also shows how a good research question can come from a flawed starting point. Darley and Latané's experiments were sound, even though the news story that inspired them was not.

Peter Fischer and his colleagues combined the results of 105 studies, covering more than seven thousand participants. They confirmed that the presence of other people reduced the chance of helping, on average. But they also found something the early studies missed: in dangerous situations, where the need was clear and the risk to the helper was real, the effect was much weaker, and sometimes reversed.

show.who: Fischer, Krueger, Greitemeyer, Vogrincic, Kastenmüller, Frey, Heene, Wicher & Kainbacher
show.what: The bystander-effect: a meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies

segments.say: That is an important refinement. In ambiguous situations, where it's not obvious that help is needed, a crowd makes people hesitate. In clear emergencies, where the danger is obvious and help is plainly needed, groups often act. The bystander effect is real, but it's not universal.

Recently, researchers have found a new kind of evidence: footage from security cameras. Instead of recreating emergencies in the laboratory, they could watch real ones, in real streets, in several countries.

Richard Philpot and his colleagues analysed CCTV footage of 219 public conflicts, in Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster. In nine out of ten of them, at least one bystander intervened in some way. And the more bystanders present, the more likely it was that someone stepped in, which is the opposite of the classic bystander effect.

show.what: Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts

segments.say: This is a remarkable finding. When people can see that something is wrong, and the danger is clear, they usually help. The finding doesn't erase the earlier research, but it places it in a wider picture. Both hold: in ambiguous situations, crowds can freeze us. In plain trouble, crowds often move.

show.title: Public conflicts where at least one bystander intervened
show.label: in CCTV footage from Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster

segments.say: The distinction explains much. When we aren't sure it's an emergency, we look to others for cues, and if they look calm, we conclude that all is well. Psychologists call this pluralistic ignorance. When it's plainly an emergency, that uncertainty disappears.

show.title: Two kinds of situation
items: Ambiguous: Is something wrong?
Ambiguous: Is it my place to act?
Clear: Someone is plainly in danger
Clear: Intervening is a recognised duty

segments.say: It's worth dwelling on this. For decades, textbooks suggested that bystanders are mostly passive. The newer evidence says the opposite for clear emergencies: most people do something, and often someone does. It doesn't mean that nobody ever fails to help. It means that helping is more common than the story told us.

Four terms from this chapter. Pluralistic ignorance is when everyone privately worries but publicly looks calm, so that each person concludes there's nothing wrong. A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies. CCTV evidence is footage of real events. And an ambiguous emergency is one where it's unclear whether help is needed.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Pluralistic ignorance
Meta-analysis
CCTV evidence
Ambiguous emergency

segments.say: Here's a small habit that follows from the research. When you're unsure whether someone needs help, ask them. A simple, Are you okay, resolves the ambiguity that keeps crowds frozen. And if you're the one who needs help, point at a specific person and say, you, in the blue jacket, please call an ambulance. Naming one person ends the diffusion of responsibility, because it turns everyone's problem into one person's task. Picture a busy station platform, a man collapses, and fifty people hesitate. One woman says, you, please call for help, and within seconds, three people are moving. That is the research in action.

show.title: A small habit to try
items: When unsure, ask out loud
Say, Are you okay?
Point to a specific person if you need help
Don't wait to see what others do

segments.say: Here is a pause to think about the crowd. Where have you seen a group freeze when something unusual happened? It might have been on a train, in a shop, in a lecture hall or at a party. Notice whether anyone spoke first, and what it was that made speaking so hard. Often, it is not fear of the situation but fear of looking foolish. We worry that we will be wrong, that it will turn out to be nothing, that the others will think we are making a fuss. Psychologists call this evaluation apprehension, and it is one of the reasons why a calm crowd is so persuasive. If you can imagine the sentence you would now say, perhaps simply, is everyone all right, then you have already begun to prepare. The silence in a crowd is rarely a decision. It is a pause that someone has to end, and it can be you.

show.title: Pause and reflect
items: Where have I seen a crowd freeze?
Did anyone speak first?
What made it easier or harder to speak?
What would I say now?

segments.say: A busy crossing in the evening light. Every person in it is both a possible helper and a possible onlooker. The research suggests that what happens next depends on whether anyone breaks the silence, and often someone does. The correction of the Genovese story is also a reminder to hold our own certainties lightly. The most repeated stories about human nature are not always the truest ones, and checking them is a form of respect for the people they describe.

If the old story left you with a bleak view of other people, put it down. The best evidence suggests that most people help when they can see that it is needed, and that the crowd, more often than we feared, contains a helper. You do not have to resolve every question this research raises. It is enough to notice the silence in a crowd the next time you meet one, and to be the person who ends it, gently and without fuss, even if only by asking a simple question.

show.sub: The crowd is not your enemy

segments.say: So what did we learn? That the famous story of thirty-eight silent witnesses did not stand up. That the bystander effect is real in ambiguous situations, but weak or reversed in clear danger. That cameras show people helping in nine of ten public conflicts. And that naming a person can break the silence.
In the next chapter, we'll meet a group of trainee priests, hurrying across a university campus to give a talk about the Good Samaritan, and a man slumped in a doorway.
